01.note: Rav Pappa came to the town of Tavakh and said he would greet any Torah scholar there. An old woman told him of Rav Shmuel, who teaches mishnayot, and blessed Rav Pappa that he should be like him; Rav Pappa concluded that Rav Shmuel must be God-fearing. Rav Shmuel slaughtered a bull in his honor and challenged him with two teachings that seem to contradict each other on burning teruma over a doubtful impurity. Rav Pappa prayed that the bull be eaten in peace and gave an answer, but Rav Shmuel knocked it down. Rav Pappa left and went to Rav Shimi bar Ashi, who asked him why he had not answered with a better case: a Samaritan who had immersed and then trod on the garments of a careful observer, which then touched teruma.
01.why: The mishna has just said that teruma is not burned over garments a Samaritan lay on, because their impurity is uncertain. The visit turns on that very ruling, and the Gemara goes on to explain Rav Shimi's answer as a double doubt.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who visits Tavakh and is challenged by his host.

people.name: Rav Shmuel
people.about: A Torah scholar in Tavakh who teaches mishnayot and hosts Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: The Sage Rav Pappa goes to afterward, who suggests the answer he could have given.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to the priests. It must be kept ritually pure; teruma that becomes impure is burned.
Plural of mishna: the short teachings of the early Sages that the Talmud discusses.
A Jew who is not careful about the rules of ritual purity, so the Sages treat his garments as likely impure.
A person known to be scrupulous about ritual purity, tithes and teruma.

02.note: A Sadducee was talking with the High Priest in the marketplace when spit flew from his mouth onto the High Priest's garments. The High Priest's face turned green, fearing his garments were now impure, and he hurried to the Sadducee's wife to ask about her practice. She told him that although they are Sadducee wives, they fear the Pharisees and show their blood to the Sages. Rabbi Yosei adds that he knew these women better than anyone and they all did so, except for one woman in his neighborhood who did not show her blood to the Sages, and she died.
02.why: The Gemara has just ruled that Sadducee women are by default treated like Samaritan women in menstrual purity. This baraita suggests they did consult the Sages; the Gemara then asks why the High Priest did not fear an ordinary man's spit.

people.name: High Priest
people.about: Unnamed; his garments are struck by a Sadducee's spit and he fears they are impure.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who says he knew the Sadducee wives well, as neighbors.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group that rejected many of the Sages' teachings, including their rules on menstrual purity.

terms.term: show their blood to the Sages
terms.meaning: A woman unsure whether a stain was menstrual blood would show it to a Sage, who ruled whether she was impure.
The Pharisees, the party of the Sages, who were careful about ritual purity.

03.note: Sheila bar Avina ruled in a real case following Rav. As Rav was dying, he told Rav Asi to go and tell Sheila the ruling was wrong, and if he did not listen, to drag him over with arguments; Rav Asi misheard it as 'excommunicate him'. After Rav died, Sheila refused, saying Rav would have told him himself, and Rav Asi excommunicated him. Sheila asked if he did not fear the fire; Rav Asi called himself a copper mortar that rot cannot touch, and Sheila answered that he was an iron pestle that smashes copper. Rav Asi fell ill, swinging between fever and chills, and died. Sheila asked his wife to prepare his shrouds so Rav Asi would not speak against him to Rav, and he too died. At the funeral the myrtle flew from one bier to the other, and people said the Sages had made peace.
03.why: The Gemara has been deriving from verses that blood from labor pains during the days of ziva is pure. The story shows that Rav, who held otherwise, took back his view before he died.

people.name: Sheila bar Avina
people.about: Rav's student, who ruled following Rav and would not accept Rav's retraction from a messenger.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher whose ruling Sheila followed; on his deathbed he sends word that it was wrong.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage Rav sends to Sheila; he mishears Rav's instruction and excommunicates Sheila.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban: the community keeps its distance from him until the ban is lifted.
A flow of blood outside a woman's regular menstrual period, which carries its own rules of ritual impurity.
A fragrant branch customarily laid on a bier at a funeral.

04.note: A man asked Rava whether one may circumcise on Shabbat, and Rava said yes. After the man left, Rava wondered how anyone could not know something so basic, so he went after him and asked how the case had actually happened. The man said he had heard the baby crying at nightfall on Friday, before Shabbat, but it was not born until Shabbat. Rava told him the baby had already put its head out, so it counted as born on Friday; a circumcision done after its proper day does not override Shabbat.
04.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Oshaya: once a baby puts its head out of the birth canal, it counts as born. Rava's case applies that rule to work out a baby's circumcision day.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who answers a man's question and then follows him to learn what really happened.

terms.meaning: The Sages' term for the birth canal. A baby whose head has come out of it counts as born.

terms.term: circumcision not at its appointed time
terms.meaning: Circumcision is done on the eighth day after birth and overrides Shabbat only then; if it is delayed, it may not be done on Shabbat.

05.note: Yusteni, daughter of Asveirus son of the Roman emperor Antoninus, came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi with questions. She asked at what age a woman may marry, and he said three years and one day; she asked at what age a woman can become pregnant, and he said twelve years and one day. She told him she had married at six and given birth at seven, and said: woe for the three years I wasted in my father's house.
05.why: The mishna has just treated three years and one day as the age from which intercourse with a girl counts in law. The Gemara then asks how Yusteni could have become pregnant so young, since a baraita assumes girls under eleven cannot conceive.

people.name: Yusteni
people.about: A gentile woman, daughter of Asveirus son of the Roman emperor Antoninus, who questions Rabbi.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sage who answers Yusteni's questions.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Talmud.

06.note: A woman came to Rabbi Akiva and told him she had had intercourse before she was three years old, and asked whether she could marry a priest. He told her she could. She then gave him a parable: a baby whose finger is dipped in honey protests the first and second time, but the third time sucks it; she meant that she had come to consent. Rabbi Akiva then told her she was unfit for the priesthood. Seeing his students look at each other, he asked what troubled them, and they said that a girl under three being fit for the priesthood is a law handed down from Moses at Sinai. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Akiva had said it only to sharpen his students.
06.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a girl under three who has had intercourse keeps her virginal status. This baraita states as a law from Sinai that she may still marry a priest, whether or not she consented.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the woman asks; he tests his students with a ruling he does not hold.

terms.meaning: Allowed to marry a priest. A priest may not marry a woman who has had certain kinds of forbidden intercourse.

terms.term: halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai
terms.meaning: A law with no source in a verse, held to have been given orally to Moses at Sinai.

07.note: Shmuel examined his maidservant for the bodily signs that mark a girl's stages of growing up, and afterward paid her four dinars for her humiliation. The Gemara explains that he was acting on his own teaching: the verse 'you may enslave them forever' means slaves were given for service, not for humiliation.
07.why: The mishna lists the signs that a girl has reached grown womanhood, and Shmuel has just explained one of them, a fold below the breast. The Gemara tells how he checked those signs himself.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who examines his maidservant for the signs of maturity and pays her for the humiliation.

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish woman held as a slave by a Jewish master.
Damages owed by someone who shames another person.

08.note: Rav Kahana's colleagues planned to let a young girl refuse her marriage even though she had had intercourse with her husband after showing the first signs of puberty. Rav Kahana reminded them of the case of Rabbi Yishmael's daughter. She came to the study hall to refuse her marriage with her son riding on her shoulders, and that same day her father's teaching allowing such a refusal was mentioned, and she wept greatly. The Sages said: should his own offspring stumble on what that righteous man taught? They voted and decided that a girl may refuse only until she grows two pubic hairs. The colleagues dropped their plan.
08.why: Rabbi Elazar has ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, who lets a girl refuse for longer; but the Gemara adds that even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that intercourse after two hairs ends her right. Rav Kahana's case shows that limit being upheld.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who stops his colleagues by recalling the case of Rabbi Yishmael's daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael's daughter
people.about: Married as a minor; she came to the study hall to refuse her marriage while already a mother.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Her father, a righteous Sage whose teaching allowed such a refusal.

terms.meaning: A girl married as a minor by her mother or brothers, after her father's death, could end the marriage simply by refusing it before she came of age.
The growth of two pubic hairs, the legal sign that a girl has reached puberty.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and decide the law.

09.note: Rabbi Yitzhak and the disciples of Rabbi Hanina allowed a young girl to refuse her marriage even though she had had intercourse with her husband after showing the first signs of puberty. Rav Shemen bar Abba reported it to Rabbi Yohanan, who reported it to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sent a constable and removed her from her second husband.
09.why: Just before, Rav Kahana's colleagues dropped a plan to rule this way once they heard of the Sages' vote. Here others actually did rule this way, and the ruling was overturned by force.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who, with Rabbi Hanina's disciples, allowed the girl to refuse.

people.name: Rav Shemen bar Abba
people.about: Reported the ruling to Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Passed the report on to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The leader who sent a constable to remove the girl from her second husband.

terms.meaning: A girl married as a minor by her mother or brothers, after her father's death, could end the marriage simply by refusing it before she came of age.

10.note: Rabbi Shimon tells how Hanina ben Hakhinai met him in Tzaidan and gave him a message for Rabbi Akiva. If Akiva said a girl may refuse her marriage only until she grows two hairs, Rabbi Shimon was to remind him that ben Shelakot had testified in front of them all at Yavne that she may refuse until the area is filled with hair, and no one had objected. When Rabbi Shimon came to Rabbi Akiva, Akiva said he did not know what this 'filling' was, did not know any ben Shelakot, and held that she may refuse until she grows two hairs.
10.why: The baraita has just listed four views on how long a girl may refuse, ending with ben Shelakot's. Rabbi Shimon's account shows Rabbi Akiva rejecting that view.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage who tells the story and carries the message to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Hanina ben Hakhinai
people.about: Meets Rabbi Shimon in Tzaidan and sends a challenge to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rejects the challenge and holds to the rule of two hairs.

people.name: ben Shelakot
people.about: Said to have testified at Yavne that a girl may refuse until the area is filled with hair.

terms.meaning: A girl married as a minor by her mother or brothers, after her father's death, could end the marriage simply by refusing it before she came of age.
The town where the Sages gathered as their central court and study house.

11.note: A woman came to Rabbi Akiva and told him she had found a blood stain. He asked whether she had a wound; she said yes, but it had healed. He asked whether it could reopen and bleed; she said yes, and Rabbi Akiva declared her pure. Seeing his students look at each other, he asked what troubled them. He explained that the Sages made the rule about stains to be lenient, not strict, since the verse says 'blood' makes a woman impure, not a stain.
11.why: The mishna has just taught that a woman may blame a stain on a wound that has scabbed over but could reopen. This incident is that ruling in practice.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who rules on the woman's stain and explains his lenient ruling to his students.

terms.meaning: Here, not in the impure state of a menstruating woman, so she is permitted to her husband.
A spot of blood found on a woman's body or clothes. By Torah law only blood felt flowing makes her impure; impurity from stains is a rule of the Sages.

12.note: Rav Hiyya bar Rav Mattana taught in Rav's name that the law follows Rabbi Nehemya. Rav Nahman objected that his father taught of a case where the Sages ruled women impure. The Gemara gives that teaching: two women grinding at a hand mill, and the rule for whom blood found beneath or between them makes impure. Then came the case itself: blood was found on the edge of a bathtub, and in another case on an olive leaf while women were lighting an oven, and the Sages ruled them impure.
12.why: Rabbi Nehemya holds that a stain found on something that cannot become impure does not make a woman impure. An olive leaf is such a thing, so Rav Nahman uses this case against ruling with him; Rav Hiyya replies that the early Sages disagreed and the ruling followed Rabbi Nehemya.

people.name: Rav Hiyya bar Rav Mattana
people.about: Teaches in Rav's name that the law follows Rabbi Nehemya.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Objects, citing a teaching from his father about a case the Sages ruled on.

terms.meaning: Here, in the impure state of a menstruating woman because of the blood found.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Talmud.

13.note: Rabbi Meir told of a sycamore tree in Kefar Sava that people believed had a corpse buried under it. They dug and found nothing. Some days later the wind uprooted the tree, and a skull was found stuck in its roots. The Sages answered him that this proves nothing: perhaps they had not searched thoroughly enough.
13.why: The mishna compares three women and a blood stain to a pile of stones that may hide part of a corpse, where Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree on whether a search can be trusted. This is the first of several cases the Gemara cites about searches that failed.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who tells of the tree, arguing that a search for a corpse cannot be relied on.

terms.meaning: An established belief that a place holds a corpse or part of one, which makes anyone who passes over it impure.

14.note: Rabbi Yosei told of a cave in Shihin that people believed held a corpse. They dug until they reached ground as smooth as a fingernail and found nothing. Some days later workers took shelter there from the rain, dug with their shovels, and found a mortar full of bones. The Sages answered him that this proves nothing: perhaps they had not searched thoroughly enough.
14.why: The Gemara is collecting cases on whether a search for a hidden corpse can be trusted, the question behind the mishna's comparison of the three women to a pile of stones. This follows Rabbi Meir's case of the sycamore and gets the same reply.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who tells of the cave in Shihin.

terms.meaning: An established belief that a place holds a corpse or part of one, which makes anyone who passes over it impure.
A heavy stone bowl used for grinding.

15.note: Abba Shaul told of a stretch of bedrock at Beit Horon that people believed held a corpse, but it was too large for the Sages to search. An old man there, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, asked for sheets, soaked them in water and spread them over the rock. Where the ground was pure the sheets stayed dry, and where it was impure they were moist. They dug there and found a large pit full of bones.
15.why: The Gemara has cited two failed searches for hidden corpses; this one shows a clever way to search. The Gemara then identifies the pit as the one Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled with the dead in the book of Jeremiah.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: The Sage who tells the story.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: An old man at Beit Horon who finds the hidden pit using wet sheets.

terms.meaning: An established belief that a place holds a corpse or part of one, which makes anyone who passes over it impure.

16.note: A rumor spread that some men from the Galilee had killed someone. They came to Rabbi Tarfon and asked him to hide them. He said: what should I do? If I do not hide you, they will see you; but if I hide you, the Rabbis said that although one must not accept malicious talk as true, one must be wary of it. Go and hide yourselves.
16.why: Rava has just taught that one must not believe malicious talk but must still be wary of it, drawn from Gedaliah, who ignored a warning and was killed. Rabbi Tarfon quotes that very rule.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The Sage the men ask for shelter; he tells them to hide themselves.

terms.meaning: Harmful talk or rumor about another person, which the Torah forbids spreading or believing.

17.note: A baraita tells that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once gave a newly married virgin four nights, spread over twelve months, during which blood after intercourse would be counted as blood from her hymen rather than menstrual blood. The Gemara then works through how those four nights could have been divided among the stages of her growing up. It settles on one night while she was a minor and three while she was a young woman, counting one night for every two months.
17.why: Rav has just said that a grown woman who has not yet menstruated gets the whole first night. The Gemara raises this case as an objection and works it out until it no longer contradicts Rav.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who gives the bride four nights.

people.name: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamya
people.about: Asked Rav a question that the Gemara quotes while working out the case.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Answers that question; his answer rules out one way of dividing the nights.

terms.meaning: Legal stages of a girl's life: a minor until about twelve, a young woman for the six months after puberty, then a grown woman.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Talmud.

17.flag: The story is a single sentence (Rabbi gave her four nights in twelve months); the rest of the STORY segments are the Gemara's legal analysis of how the nights were divided.

18.note: Minyamin Saksana was on his way to Shmuel's town, planning to rule as Rav had: to let a grown woman attribute bleeding to her hymen for the whole first night, even if she had already menstruated. He thought Rav made no distinction between a woman who had menstruated and one who had not. He died on the road before he arrived. Shmuel applied to Rav the verse 'No mishap shall befall the righteous.'
18.why: Rav ruled that a grown woman gets the whole first night only if she has not yet menstruated. Minyamin was about to apply it without that condition, and his death is read as God keeping Rav's teaching from being misused.

people.name: Minyamin Saksana
people.about: A Sage who misread Rav's ruling and died on the way to apply it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage to whose town Minyamin was going; he recites a verse about Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Minyamin misunderstood.

terms.meaning: Here, a woman who has already had menstrual bleeding before her marriage.

19.note: A woman who bled whenever she had intercourse came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He told Abdon to go and frighten her. Abdon did, and a mass of clotted blood fell from her. Rabbi said: this woman is cured.
19.why: The baraita under discussion says that a woman who bleeds from intercourse on three occasions must be divorced. This case shows that such a woman can sometimes be cured.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whom the woman consults.

people.name: Abdon
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi sends to frighten the woman.

20.note: A woman who bled whenever she had intercourse came to Shmuel. He told Rav Dimi bar Yosef to go and frighten her. Rav Dimi did, but nothing fell from her. Shmuel said she was a woman who fills with blood and lets it out, and such a woman has no cure.
20.why: Just before, Rabbi cured a woman the same way, when a mass of blood fell from her. Here the same method fails, showing it does not always work.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage the woman consults; he sends Rav Dimi to frighten her.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: Sent by Shmuel to frighten the woman.
